title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation fraud in which AI-generated content was used to fabricate a fake interview between two real public figures, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock and ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler, to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform called Boulder Sparhaven. The failure sits entirely outside any legitimate AI deployment, as the technology was used by scammers rather than misused by a company deploying it for a stated purpose. The fabricated article circulated online, and the convincingness of the output is what made detection difficult for ordinary consumers.

ASIC's figures show the scale of the broader pattern: the regulator removed 19,400 scams in the relevant period, up 182 percent, including over 7,000 fake investment platforms, with well-known Australians including the Prime Minister and several public figures regularly impersonated. The failure mode is deliberate misuse of deepfake image and video generation to produce fraudulent endorsements, not a malfunction of a deployed system. Catching individual instances would require either platform-level detection before distribution or consumer-level verification of credentials, neither of which is currently reliable at the speed and volume involved.

What is not established is whether any specific AI tool or company is responsible for producing the fake content, and ASIC's warnings and removed content count are regulatory findings, not court verdicts on individual fraud cases.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler has surfaced as part of a rising scam trend. The fabricated story promoted Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform, through the false confrontation. However, the interview never actually occurred. This type of deception represents a growing problem identified by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, which found that artificial intelligence technology is making investment scams increasingly convincing and difficult to detect.

ASIC's latest research reveals that scammers are building elaborate webs of deception using deepfake images and videos of well-known Australians. Last year, the regulator removed 19,400 scams overall, up 182 percent, including 7,051 fake investment platforms. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, politician Pauline Hanson, businessman Dick Smith, and billionaire Gina Rinehart are among frequently impersonated figures. ASIC warns consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers independently and to avoid investing with companies unable to provide verifiable credentials, while Alan Kohler argues that platforms distributing this content should face heavy financial penalties.
